title: A2 — Highly available and fault-tolerant architectures
bodyMarkdown:
## Highly available and fault-tolerant architectures

Exam task **2.2**. Every drill for this task is built from the concepts below — read this before you attempt them. Task 2.1 already covered ALB/NLB mechanics, SQS, read replicas, and Auto Scaling policies in depth; this lesson refers back to those briefly and focuses on availability and disaster recovery.

### K01 — AWS global infrastructure

An **AWS Region** is an independent geographic area containing multiple **Availability Zones (AZs)** — one or more physically separate data centers with their own power, cooling, and networking, linked to the other AZs in the Region by low-latency connections. Spreading a workload's subnets and instances across at least two AZs is the baseline technique for surviving the loss of a single data center, at no extra design cost. A Region failure is a rarer class of event that only a second Region can protect against.

**Amazon Route 53** is AWS's highly available, global DNS service, offering several **routing policies**: **simple** for one resource; **weighted** to split traffic across resources by a percentage; **latency-based** to send each client to the lowest-latency Region; **geolocation** to route by client location, for compliance or localization; **geoproximity** to route by resource location with an optional bias to shift traffic between resources; **IP-based** to route by the client's IP address using a customer-supplied CIDR map; **multivalue answer** to return up to eight healthy records at random; and **failover** for active-passive DNS failover (K06). Every policy but simple can pair with a Route 53 **health check** so an unhealthy endpoint stops appearing in Route 53's answers.

**Exam tip:** decide the failure scope first — "one data center" means Multi-AZ is enough; "the whole Region" means a second Region and one of these Route 53 policies in front of both.

### K02 — AWS Managed Services with appropriate use cases

A purpose-built managed AI service ships with AWS's own multi-AZ resilience already built in, removing a whole category of infrastructure-availability work from your design. **Amazon Comprehend** runs natural-language processing (sentiment, entities, key phrases, language detection) against text submitted through an API call, with no model training infrastructure to run or patch. **Amazon Polly** turns text into lifelike speech with neural text-to-speech voices, again through an API call, and the generated audio can be cached and replayed at no extra cost. Neither service asks you to provision, scale, or fail over anything yourself.

**Exam tip:** "no servers to patch, and it's already resilient because AWS runs it" points at a managed AI service like Comprehend or Polly, not a model you host and fail over yourself on EC2.

### K03 — Basic networking concepts

A **route table** holds the rules that determine where traffic leaving a subnet is sent; every subnet is associated with exactly one route table (the VPC's main route table, by default). Route tables matter for availability because a route to the internet or another network normally points at an AZ-specific resource such as a NAT gateway — a route table in one AZ that points at a NAT gateway in a different AZ creates a cross-AZ dependency that breaks if that AZ fails. The resilient pattern is one NAT gateway and one route table per AZ, so each AZ's outbound path survives independently of the others.

**Exam tip:** "each AZ must keep working if another AZ fails" points to a route table and a NAT gateway per AZ, not one shared NAT gateway referenced by every AZ's table.

### K04 — Disaster recovery (DR) strategies

AWS defines four DR strategies for recovering a workload in another Region, in increasing order of cost and complexity and decreasing order of RTO and RPO:

- **Backup and restore** — RPO in hours, RTO in 24 hours or less (point-in-time recovery can push RPO to about 5 minutes). Back up data and infrastructure-as-code to the recovery Region; at disaster time, deploy the infrastructure, deploy the code, and restore the data.
- **Pilot light** — RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes. Core data stores stay running and replicating in the recovery Region; compute is not deployed until needed, then created from existing configuration.
- **Warm standby** — RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes. A scaled-down but fully functional copy runs continuously in the recovery Region with live data; recovery just scales it up to full production load.
- **Multi-site active/active** — RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero. The workload runs in, and actively serves traffic from, multiple Regions at once, requiring write-conflict handling between replicas.

**RPO** (recovery point objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured backward in time from the disaster; **RTO** (recovery time objective) is how long the workload can be down before it must be back.

**Exam tip:** memorize the ordering — backup and restore is cheapest and slowest to recover; active/active is the most expensive and the fastest; pilot light and warm standby sit between them, distinguished by whether compute is already running.

### K05 — Distributed design patterns

The decoupling and redundancy patterns from task 2.1 (queues, event buses, stateless tiers behind a load balancer) apply directly to HA: a distributed design spreads redundant copies of each component across AZs or Regions and removes any dependency on one specific instance or AZ, so a single failure degrades capacity rather than taking the whole system down. A stateless application tier behind a health-checked load balancer is the clearest example — any healthy instance in any AZ can serve any request.

**Exam tip:** "one component fails, the system keeps serving traffic" is a distributed, redundant design; a single scaled-up instance handling everything is the opposite of this pattern.

### K06 — Failover strategies

Three layers of failover work together in a resilient architecture:

- **Amazon RDS Multi-AZ automatic failover** — the DB instance's endpoint transparently repoints to the standby, without any DNS or application change needed.
- **Route 53 failover routing**, backed by **health checks**, implements active-passive DNS failover: Route 53 monitors an endpoint's health and stops returning it in DNS answers once it fails, routing clients to the secondary resource instead.
- **Auto Scaling and Elastic Load Balancing health checks** replace unhealthy instances automatically and stop sending traffic to instances that fail their checks, healing a compute fleet without human action.

RDS itself offers several database HA options that are easy to mix up. A **Multi-AZ DB instance** keeps one non-readable standby purely for automatic failover. A **Multi-AZ DB cluster** keeps two readable standbys across three AZs, adding read capacity on top of that same failover protection. A **read replica** (task 2.1) is an asynchronous, promotable copy built to offload reads, not to fail over automatically. **Aurora Replicas** are Aurora's own low-lag read replicas, which also serve as automatic in-Region failover targets. **Aurora Global Database** extends an Aurora cluster with secondary, read-only clusters in other Regions, promotable if the primary Region is lost.

**Exam tip:** "the DNS answer itself must change to point at a backup site" is Route 53 failover routing; "survive an AZ loss with no read capacity added" is a Multi-AZ DB instance, while "survive an AZ loss and also get extra readers" is a Multi-AZ DB cluster.

### K07 — Immutable infrastructure

**Immutable infrastructure** means no in-place updates, patches, or configuration changes to running production resources — every change ships as a new image or template that replaces the old resource entirely. This makes a deployment atomic: it either completes in full or leaves the previous, known-good version untouched, with no partially-patched state to debug. It also eliminates configuration drift between instances, and rollback is simply relaunching the previous image rather than undoing a change in place.

**Exam tip:** "roll back instantly to a known-good state" and "no configuration drift between instances" both point to immutable infrastructure, not patching servers where they run.

### K08 — Load balancing concepts

Task 2.1 covers ALB and NLB mechanics; the HA-specific points are health checks and cross-zone balancing. An **Application Load Balancer's health checks** continuously probe registered targets and stop routing to any target that fails them, which is what makes a multi-AZ fleet self-healing from the traffic side. **Cross-zone load balancing**, on by default for an ALB, spreads requests evenly across every healthy target in every enabled AZ rather than only the targets in the AZ that received the request — without it, an AZ with fewer healthy targets takes a disproportionate share of load per instance.

**Exam tip:** "traffic is balanced evenly across AZs no matter how many healthy targets each AZ has" is cross-zone load balancing.

### K09 — Proxy concepts

**Amazon RDS Proxy** sits between an application and its RDS or Aurora database, pooling and multiplexing many short-lived client connections onto fewer database connections — this stops a fleet of Lambda functions or a busy web tier from exhausting the database's connection limit. RDS Proxy also improves availability during a failover: it holds client-side connections open and transparently switches them to the new writer, cutting the failover time the application perceives by up to 66% versus reconnecting from scratch. The application changes nothing except its connection string.

**Exam tip:** "too many short-lived connections are overwhelming the database" and "shorten how long the app is affected during a failover" both point to RDS Proxy.

### K10 — Service quotas and throttling

Every AWS service enforces **service quotas** per account and Region, and a standby DR environment that normally runs scaled down can hide a quota gap it would only hit at full failover scale — for example, an EC2 vCPU limit in the recovery Region that pilot light or warm standby never exercised at small size. Request the needed quota increases in the recovery Region ahead of time, through the Service Quotas console or API, rather than discovering the gap during an actual disaster. **Throttling** is a service rejecting or delaying requests once a rate limit is hit; workloads should retry with backoff rather than assume every call succeeds.

**Exam tip:** "the failover Region couldn't scale up when the disaster happened" is a service-quota gap in the recovery Region — fix it by requesting the increase before it's needed, not after.

### K11 — Storage options and characteristics

Durability and replication scope differ by storage type. An **Amazon EBS volume** replicates within a single AZ only — an io2 volume is designed for 99.999% durability, but that protects against drive failure, not AZ loss, so cross-AZ or cross-Region durability needs a snapshot copied elsewhere. **Amazon EFS**, as a Regional file system, replicates data and metadata across all AZs in the Region automatically, giving it higher built-in availability than a single EBS volume. **Amazon S3** stores objects redundantly across at least three AZs by default and is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability — the exception is **S3 One Zone-IA**, which trades that redundancy for a lower price by using a single AZ.

**Exam tip:** "durable across the loss of an AZ with no extra work" is S3 (excluding One Zone-IA) or EFS; a bare EBS volume needs snapshots to reach that bar.

### K12 — Workload visibility

**Amazon CloudWatch** collects the metrics, logs, and alarms an HA design depends on to know when something is unhealthy and needs to fail over. **AWS X-Ray** adds distributed tracing on top of that: it traces a single request across multiple services, builds a service map, and pinpoints which downstream call in a chain introduced latency or an error — something a per-resource CloudWatch metric alone cannot show.

**Exam tip:** "find which specific service in a chain of calls is causing the slowdown" is X-Ray; "alarm when one metric crosses a threshold" is CloudWatch.

### S01 — Determining automation strategies to ensure infrastructure integrity

Automate away the chance that a human hand-edits a running resource: deploy through infrastructure as code so every environment is reproducible from a template; deploy application changes as immutable infrastructure (K07) so there is nothing to drift; let Auto Scaling health checks replace failed instances instead of paging someone; and use AWS Backup's policy-based schedules (S05) instead of ad hoc manual snapshots. Each removes one path by which a resource could silently end up undocumented and unrecoverable.

**Exam tip:** if a design still requires someone to log in and manually fix or patch a production resource, the automation strategy is incomplete.

### S02 — Determining the AWS services required to provide a highly available and/or fault-tolerant architecture across AWS Regions or Availability Zones

Inside one Region, reach for Multi-AZ subnets, an ALB or NLB spreading traffic across AZs, an Auto Scaling group spanning AZs, and RDS Multi-AZ for the database. Across Regions, reach for **Aurora Global Database** (K06), **DynamoDB global tables** (multi-Region, multi-active replication; defaults to multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC), with an MRSC same-account option for multi-Region strong consistency, and conflicting writes resolved last-writer-wins), **S3 Cross-Region Replication**, a Route 53 policy that spans the Regions, and **AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery** or AWS Backup's cross-Region copy for the rest of the stack.

**Exam tip:** "must keep working after losing an entire Region" rules out AZ-only options and calls for the Region-spanning services in this list.

### S03 — Identifying metrics based on business requirements to deliver a highly available solution

Turn a business statement into a number before picking a design. Availability is usually expressed as a percentage of uptime — "the nines" — where 99.9% allows roughly 8.7 hours of downtime a year and 99.99% allows roughly 52 minutes; RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime and RPO the maximum acceptable data loss, both measured from CloudWatch metrics and health-check history, not guessed. Match the metric's strictness to the workload: an internal nightly batch job can tolerate an RTO of hours, while a customer-facing checkout page usually cannot.

**Exam tip:** convert "can't be down more than X minutes" into an explicit RTO, then pick the DR strategy from K04 whose RTO fits — choosing a stricter, costlier strategy than the stated requirement is a wrong answer just as much as choosing one that's too slow.

### S04 — Implementing designs to mitigate single points of failure

A **single point of failure (SPOF)** is any one component whose failure takes the whole system down: one EC2 instance outside an Auto Scaling group, a deployment confined to a single AZ, one NAT gateway shared by every AZ's route table, or a database with no Multi-AZ standby. Mitigate a SPOF by duplicating it across AZs (and Regions, when required), fronting it with a load balancer or Auto Scaling group so any healthy copy can take over, or replacing it with a managed service already redundant by design, such as S3 or DynamoDB.

**Exam tip:** whenever an architecture diagram shows exactly one instance of something sitting in the path every request must pass through, that single instance is the SPOF the question wants you to fix.

### S05 — Implementing strategies to ensure the durability and availability of data

**AWS Backup** centralizes backup automation across many services — EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, and more — with policy-based schedules, lifecycle transitions to cheaper storage, and cross-account or cross-Region copy, replacing custom per-service snapshot scripts. **AWS Backup Vault Lock** can additionally lock a vault's retention settings in governance mode, removable by users with sufficient IAM permissions, or in compliance mode, which becomes immutable — unchangeable and undeletable by any user, including the root user — once a mandatory cooling-off period of at least 72 hours expires. **Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication** asynchronously copies objects to a bucket in another Region, useful for durability, compliance, and serving a distant read audience with lower latency. Combine continuous replication (CRR, DynamoDB global tables, Aurora Global Database) for the lowest possible RPO with scheduled AWS Backup snapshots for point-in-time recovery, since replication alone still propagates an accidental delete to every replica.

**Exam tip:** "must be able to restore to a specific point in time after an accidental delete" calls for a scheduled backup, not replication alone — replication would have already copied the deletion.

### S06 — Selecting an appropriate DR strategy to meet business requirements

Apply the K04 catalog to the stated numbers and budget: cheap and tolerant of hours of downtime points to backup and restore; minutes of RTO on a tight budget points to pilot light; minutes of RTO with seconds of RPO points to warm standby; near-zero RTO and RPO regardless of which Region is lost points to multi-site active/active, accepting its cost and write-conflict handling. Match the strategy to the numbers first, and use cost as the tiebreaker — don't default to the most resilient option unless the stated RTO/RPO demands it.

**Exam tip:** find the RTO and RPO numbers in the question stem, line them up against K04's ranges, and pick the cheapest strategy that still satisfies both.

### S07 — Using AWS services that improve the reliability of legacy applications and applications not built for the cloud

When the application's code cannot change, reach for services that sit in front of or alongside it instead of a rewrite. **AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS)** continuously replicates on-premises or cloud servers at the block level into a low-cost staging area and can launch fully booted recovery instances on AWS within minutes for a drill or a real failover, with no source-code changes required. **RDS Proxy** improves resiliency for a legacy application that opens many short-lived, unpooled database connections, again without touching its code. An **ALB or NLB** in front of a legacy fleet adds health-checked failover the application was never written to do itself, and **AWS Backup** adds automated protection for its storage.

**Exam tip:** "the application cannot be modified" is the signal to reach for a drop-in service such as AWS DRS, RDS Proxy, or a load balancer, not a re-architecture.

### S08 — Using purpose-built AWS services for workloads

Reach for the service already built multi-AZ or multi-Region instead of re-implementing that resilience by hand: **AWS Backup** instead of custom snapshot scripts, **DynamoDB global tables** instead of hand-rolled cross-Region replication with conflict resolution, **Aurora Global Database** instead of manual cross-Region replicas and promotion runbooks, **Route 53 health-checked failover** instead of a custom heartbeat-and-DNS script, and **AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery** instead of a homegrown replication agent.

**Exam tip:** when a distractor describes building and maintaining your own replication, health-check, or backup tooling on EC2, the purpose-built managed service doing the same job is almost always the intended answer.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
